name: Mehrabian 7-38-55 rule

card.summary: A communication claim that words, tone and facial expression carry 7%, 38% and 55% of impact, used to argue that how you look and sound matters most.
card.note: Original findings apply to conveying feelings and attitudes only.

quick.overview:
The 7-38-55 rule attributes 7% of a message's impact to words, 38% to tone of voice and 55% to facial expression. It is cited in appearance and presence circles to argue that looks, voice and expression do most of the work in first impressions.

It comes from two 1967 studies by psychologist Albert Mehrabian that used single spoken words with different tones and facial photographs. Mehrabian himself said the numbers apply to communicating feelings and attitudes, not communication in general.
quick.how: People use it as a rationale to work on facial expression, vocal tone and grooming rather than script alone. It is a framing, not a routine.
quick.risks: Misapplying the percentages to all communication overstates them; later studies reported different ratios.

lead: The Mehrabian 7-38-55 rule is the claim that in communication 7% of meaning comes from words, 38% from tone of voice and 55% from facial expression. In appearance communities it is cited to show that visible cues such as expression and presence dominate first impressions.[1]

The figures come from two 1967 studies, "Decoding of Inconsistent Communications" and "Inference of Attitudes from Nonverbal Communication in Two Channels," which Mehrabian combined into the ratio.[1]
Mehrabian stated that the formula, "Total Liking = 7% Verbal Liking + 38% Vocal Liking + 55% Facial Liking," applies only when a speaker discusses feelings or attitudes.[1]

chain: Facial expression and tone are emphasised
Positive attitude is conveyed more clearly
angle.text: The rule is used to justify attention to expression, voice and grooming. It is a framework for reasoning about impressions rather than a technique.

paras: Both studies had participants judge positive or negative feelings from single words like "dear" or "terrible" delivered in different tones; the second paired facial photographs with recorded tone and found about a 3:2 ratio between the channels. Only women took part.[1]

No studies found of the rule as an appearance intervention. Related research on its premise: a 1970 study of dominant and submissive attitudes found nonverbal cues had about 4.3 times the impact of verbal cues, while a 1992 study of happy and sad moods found flat-toned words about four times more influential than facial expressions.[1]

Commentators note the setup was artificial, the studies were combined questionably, only liking was tested and posture was not examined; the figures are frequently misquoted in communication seminars.[1]

timeline.event: Mehrabian publishes the two studies behind the ratio.[1]
